domain: Safety Engineering / Organizational Learning / High-Reliability Organizations
topic_summary: Analysis of whether simulation-based training adequately maintains catastrophe-avoidance competence in aviation (stall recovery, CRM) and nuclear (meltdown response) sectors across decades without recurring real catastrophes. The kernel contest is whether drills count as the exercise that keeps competence alive, or whether only actual catastrophic events do.

key_entities: FAA/EASA (regulatory bodies mandating simulator training as sufficient)
Airlines and nuclear plant operators (institutional implementers)
Simulator manufacturers (CORYS, L3Harris, APS - technology providers)
Pilots and nuclear operators (practitioners with embodied competence)
Colgan Air/Air France 447 crashes (catastrophe anchors driving regulatory change)
Line audits vs jeopardy simulation (assessment mechanism tension)
key_tensions: Regulatory mandate (simulation sufficient) vs practitioner skepticism (real aircraft/events irreplaceable)
Skill retention via simulation vs skill decay without real-world exercise (2-month deterioration window)
Fidelity of simulation vs transfer-of-training concerns (negative transfer, idealized conditions)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Catastrophe-avoidance competence must be exercised to remain occupied; the shared commitment is that competence atrophies without exercise
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC) claim authority to certify what counts as adequate exercise; practitioners claim authority grounded in embodied experience

readings.commitment: Simulation with high fidelity and debriefing constitutes adequate exercise of the competence kernel
readings.authority_grounding: Regulatory mandate + learning science evidence (skill retention studies, debriefing effectiveness)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence maintained via scheduled simulation cycles; catastrophe-free decades validate the reading; regulatory compliance sufficient

readings.commitment: Only real catastrophic events (or near-misses) provide the irreducible exercise that maintains competence
readings.authority_grounding: Practitioner embodied knowledge + transfer-of-training skepticism + real-world variability claims
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence kernel atrophies during catastrophe-free periods despite simulation; first real event reveals decay; 'muscle memory' vs 'knowing about' distinction

readings.commitment: Simulation is necessary but insufficient; competence requires both simulation foundation and periodic real-world anchoring (line operations, non-jeopardy audits, actual aircraft time)
readings.authority_grounding: Synthesis position grounded in 'complementary not replacement' evidence + skill decay timelines + negative transfer concerns
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence maintained via hybrid regime; pure simulation creates fragile equilibrium; pure real-world exercise ethically/practically impossible; line audits and real aircraft time bridge the gap

axiom_contradictions.basis: One holds that high-fidelity representation with debriefing is structurally equivalent to the real event for competence maintenance; the other holds that embodied experience of actual physical systems under real stakes is irreducible and cannot be simulated. No single framework can hold both 'simulation is adequate' and 'only real catastrophe maintains competence' simultaneously.

omegas.description: Does the 'drills as proxy-catastrophe' formulation collapse the reading distinction? Evidence suggests NO: practitioners distinguish 'muscle memory' from 'knowing about,' line audits reveal non-jeopardy performance gaps, and real aircraft time remains structurally distinct from simulation. The readings remain operationally meaningful.
omegas.source: Kernel contest specification + research evidence on complementary-not-replacement

omegas.description: Decades of catastrophe-free operations could validate simulation_as_adequate_exercise OR mask competence decay that would only surface in the next real catastrophe. The absence of catastrophe is not evidence of competence retention—it is absence of the test.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + practitioner skepticism evidence

omegas.description: Is the 'feel of turbulence' and 'physical cues' claim a mountain (irreducible physics) or a rope (coordination around shared practitioner norms)? If mountain, catastrophe_as_necessary_anchor reading gains structural weight. If rope, simulation fidelity improvements could close the gap.
omegas.source: F03 (Hasty Generalization) + practitioner testimony on real vs simulated aircraft

omegas.description: Line audits under non-jeopardy conditions reveal crew coordination gaps not visible in simulation. This suggests a fourth reading: 'routine operations as competence anchor' distinct from both simulation and catastrophe. Deferred for token budget but structurally significant.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + line audit evidence
